questions.q: In the example where var y = 2; is declared inside an if block, why is y still accessible outside that block afterward?
options: JavaScript doesn't actually support if blocks
var variables are always global regardless of where they're declared
y was declared twice accidentally
var is scoped to the nearest function, not the block, so it "leaks" out of if blocks and loops
questions.explain: var's function-level scoping means it isn't contained by the if block's curly braces the way let and const are.

questions.q: In a JavaScript class, what does the constructor do?
options: It is optional and never actually runs
It deletes the instance when the program ends
It runs once, when a new instance is created with `new`, typically to set up that instance's own data
It runs every time any method on the class is called
questions.explain: The constructor initializes a new instance's state exactly once, at creation time.

questions.q: What does const status = balance > 0 ? "funded" : "empty"; do?
options: It assigns both "funded" and "empty" at once
It always assigns "funded" regardless of balance
It's a ternary expression: a compact if/else that assigns "funded" if balance > 0 is true, otherwise "empty"
It throws a syntax error because ternary expressions don't exist in JavaScript
questions.explain: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse evaluates the condition once and assigns exactly one of the two values.

questions.q: Inside a class method, what does the `this` keyword refer to?
options: The specific instance the method was called on, and its own data
The global window object, always
The class definition itself, shared across all instances
Nothing — `this` is not valid inside a class
questions.explain: Each instance created with `new` has its own data, and `this` inside a method refers to that specific instance.
